payload.rationale: As of September 17, 2026 (roughly 71% of the year), there are 3,471 confirmed US measles cases. To exceed the 6,000 threshold, more than 2,529 additional cases must be recorded in the remaining 105 days. This would require the average incidence rate to nearly double, from about 13.4 cases per day year-to-date to over 24 cases per day. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that measles outbreaks typically peak in the late winter and spring, making a massive surge in the fall less likely, so the actual probability might be even lower. The strongest reason this estimate could be too low is that measles is highly contagious and 95% of the current cases are outbreak-associated; a new, large outbreak in a densely populated, undervaccinated community could cause a sudden and explosive spike in cases before the year ends.
limitations: Relies on provisional CDC data which may be subject to reporting lags and revisions.
Assumes historical seasonality patterns hold, which may not be true during a major resurgence.
Lacks detailed epidemiological modeling of current outbreak trajectories.
